rationale: Start with a broad, mid-strength scouting gradient at moderate temperature to elute all 10 compounds if possible while revealing overall retention spread and crowding. This gives a balanced first map of the mixture before narrowing phi range, gradient time, or temperature.

All 10 compounds are already fully resolved, so the only clear improvement is reducing analysis time while preserving resolution. A shorter gradient with the same composition range and temperature should compress the run and likely increase CRF unless the middle cluster becomes too crowded.

The 12 min gradient is very fast but slightly over-compresses the central cluster, giving a near-coelution for peaks 6 and 7. A small increase in gradient time should selectively restore resolution in that region while keeping total run time short and potentially improving CRF further.

The trend from 12 to 14 min shows the limiting pair improves as the gradient is slightly lengthened, and there is still no time penalty. Testing 16 min should reveal whether a bit more spreading lifts the last pair above the critical threshold and reaches the maximum CRF.

Since 14 min is near-optimal in time, the next lever is selectivity around the crowded mid-eluting cluster. Lowering phi1 slightly should flatten the late part of the gradient and may open peaks 6 and 7 enough to reach full resolution without increasing run time too much.

A nearby confirmatory condition tests how robust the optimum is to a slightly shallower final gradient strength while keeping the same successful timing. This should maintain full elution and may show whether the separation has a small plateau of CRF 1.000 methods around the current optimum.

Now that phi1 = 0.85 gave full resolution at 14 min, the key question is whether this improved selectivity can support a shorter gradient and still keep CRF at 1.000. Testing 12 min directly probes whether run time can be reduced without reintroducing the 6/7 overlap seen at phi1 = 0.90.

The optimum appears centered at phi1 = 0.85, tG = 14, so a small increase in gradient time checks whether there is a plateau of maximum-CRF conditions on the slower side. This maps robustness around the current optimum without changing selectivity variables.

With phi1 and tG near optimum, changing phi0 is the remaining straightforward way to test local robustness and possibly ease the early gradient steepness seen by the crowded middle group. A slightly higher starting organic may subtly alter selectivity while likely keeping all 10 compounds within the no-penalty time window.

A further small increase in phi0 explores whether the 1.000 plateau extends to even shorter retention while preserving the critical 6/7 resolution. Since phi0 = 0.15 improved run time slightly with full resolution, phi0 = 0.20 is the logical next local step.

Two conditions now achieve CRF 1.000, so the next useful check is whether the optimum plateau extends in phi1 at the better phi0 = 0.15 setting. Raising phi1 slightly may preserve full resolution while shortening the tail of the chromatogram further.

phi0 = 0.15 appears favorable, and testing the symmetric decrease in phi1 around the known optimum will define the local 1.000 region. This checks whether slightly lower phi1 improves the critical 6/7 pair enough to offset any small time increase.

Since composition adjustments have mapped a narrow optimum region, temperature is the remaining major selectivity variable worth probing near the best condition. A modest drop to 35 C may improve the limiting 6/7 selectivity while likely keeping the run inside the no-penalty window.

Lowering temperature strongly worsened selectivity by creating a new 5/6 overlap, so checking the opposite direction is the most informative next step. A modest increase to 45 C may preserve or improve the successful 40 C pattern while defining the temperature dependence around the optimum.

At 45 C the main problem is a severe 6/7 compression, and the lower-phi0 condition previously gave the largest 6/7 separation at 40 C. Testing phi0 = 0.10 at 45 C probes whether starting weaker can recover selectivity under the hotter condition and clarify the interaction between temperature and initial solvent strength.

Both hotter and cooler temperatures changed selectivity enough to create new overlaps, so a shorter gradient at 35 C is a useful orthogonal check of whether time compression can move the critical crossover away from the disastrous 5/6 overlap. This helps characterize the selectivity landscape around the temperature-sensitive region while staying near the known good composition.

The best region is clearly at 40 C and phi1 = 0.85 with only subtle dependence on phi0, so testing the lower bound of phi0 completes the local map around the optimum. This checks whether starting still weaker further improves the critical middle-pair spacing without pushing the run out of the no-penalty zone.

The optimum is already found, so the best use of remaining injections is to map broader behavior; 35 and 45 C both changed selectivity dramatically, so probing the lower temperature limit defines that trend. This will show whether the 5/6 coelution at 35 C becomes even more severe or whether a nonmonotonic temperature effect appears.

The remaining unexplored major axis is the upper temperature limit, and the strong temperature sensitivity suggests it is worth defining the full trend. Running 60 C will show whether selectivity continues to deteriorate monotonically above 45 C or if another crossover region appears.

At 40 C the only unresolved local question near the optimum is whether phi0 has a narrow maximum around 0.10–0.15 or degrades gradually upward. Testing phi0 = 0.25 extends that trend and helps bracket the upper edge of the 1.000 region.

A longer gradient at 35 C tests whether the severe low-temperature 5/6 overlap is mainly a kinetic compression issue that can be rescued by added gradient time. This is the cleanest way to separate temperature from gradient-steepness effects in the low-temperature regime.

Since extending the gradient at 35 C did not rescue the low-temperature crossover, the analogous 45 C experiment will show whether the high-temperature 6/7 overlap is likewise intrinsic rather than due to gradient steepness. This completes the paired temperature–gradient comparison around the optimum.

The best conditions cluster near phi1 = 0.85, but phi1 = 0.80 still gave full resolution with only a small time penalty. Testing phi1 = 0.75 maps the lower edge more completely and checks whether additional flattening of the late gradient might retain full resolution while remaining competitively fast.

With only two injections left and the optimum already found, a useful remaining gap is whether shortening the gradient at 45 C worsens the same 6/7 crossover or shifts the limiting pair. This further defines the hot-condition selectivity surface around the known bad region.

For the final run, the only nearby unexplored composition point around the 40 C optimum is a higher phi1 limit. This completes the local phi1 map around the known best region and tests whether the upper edge degrades similarly to phi1 = 0.90 or more strongly.
